Coalition Formation with Limited Information Sharing for Local
Energy Management*
Luke Rickard1, Paola Falugi1and Eric C. Kerrigan2
Abstract— Distributed energy systems with prosumers re-
quire new methods for coordinating energy exchange among
agents. Coalitional control provides a framework in which
agents form groups to cooperatively reduce costs; however, ex-
isting bottom-up coalition-formation methods typically require
full information sharing, raising privacy concerns and imposing
significant computational overhead.
In this work, we propose a limited information coalition-
formation algorithm that requires only limited aggregate in-
formation exchange among agents. By constructing an upper
bound on the value of candidate coalitions, we eliminate the
need to solve optimisation problems for each potential merge,
significantly reducing computational complexity while limiting
information exchange. We prove that the proposed method
guarantees cost no greater than that of decentralised operation.
Coalition strategies are optimised using a distributed ap-
proach based on the Alternating Direction Method of Multi-
pliers (ADMM), further limiting information sharing within
coalitions. We embed the framework within a model predictive
control scheme and evaluate it on real-world data, demon-
strating improved economic performance over decentralised
control with substantially lower computational cost than full-
information approaches.
I. INTRODUCTION
Energy production around the world is currently undergo-
ing a significant paradigm shift from fossil fuels to renewable
energy sources. One part of this transition is the change
from relying on a few large, high-capacity power plants to
depending on many smaller, widely distributed generation
units [1]. In particular, we are interested in the rise of
“prosumers”, participants in the energy market who both
consume and produce electricity [2], [3]. This motivates
exploring novel control techniques better suited to the new
energy generation landscape.
One promising area of research that leverages this shift in
generation iscoalitional control[4], [5]. Coalitional control
is an approach that considers grouping entities involved in
a large problem into separate coalitions that can be solved
separately. We refer to this initial grouping of agents, before
the subproblems are solved, as coalition formation. For
the grid scenario, coalitional control can involve buildings
agreeing to trade energy with one another, aiming to pay
less than they would by interacting only with the grid.
Forming coalitions allows agents to reduce their individual
costs without incurring large computational or communi-
cation overheads, and without sharing full local informa-
tion with agents outside the coalition (once coalitions are

in the case of the smart grid, can lead to vulnerabilities,
allowing attackers to infer various household traits [6], [7].
However, while recent work that has explored bottom-up
coalition formation [5] addresses computational complexity,
it still requires full information sharing during coalition
formation, negating these privacy benefits. In particular, the
technique in [5] required solving the complete optimisation
problem for every pair of agents, requiring each agent to
broadcast all optimisation variables and constraints to all
other agents. Not only does this introduce privacy concerns,
but it also represents a computational bottleneck. We seek
a “limited information sharing” scheme that avoids sharing
full local demand, generation, storage, and constraint data.
Instead, agents only share tentative grid trade plans during
coalition formation, and coalition trade plans afterwards.
This reduces information shared and computational costs.
We make use of Model Predictive Control (MPC) tech-
niques to optimise energy trades and battery charging pro-
files, with forecasted energy usage and production for a day
ahead. MPC has been studied in this context in [8], but it is
limited to a single building, whereas we consider a group of
buildings that may form into coalitions. Our work extends
upon current extensions of MPC to coalitions [9], [10] by re-
ducing the amount of information shared (and computational
requirements) for each possible coalition formation step, and
dynamically updates coalitions at every time step to account
for changing conditions.
Coalitional control aligns with techniques in distributed
control, such as the Alternating Direction Method of Mul-
tipliers [11], explored for energy grids in [12], [13]. While
distributed control provides a powerful framework for op-
timising systems composed of multiple agents, it typically
assumes a fixed interaction structure and does not address
how agents should be grouped. In many applications, form-
ing such groups is desirable to limit information sharing, re-
duce computational burden, or manage communication costs.
Coalitional control addresses this by determining groups of
agents (coalitions) that can then optimise their decisions
jointly, e.g., using distributed optimisation techniques.
In this work, we propose a coalition formation framework
that reduces both computational complexity and information
sharing. The approach enables agents to evaluate potential
coalition merges using only limited, aggregate information,
without requiring full knowledge of local models or solving
a full optimisation problem for each candidate merge. The
main contributions of this paper are as follows:

D. Within Coalition Optimisation
Once a coalition structure is formed, we must also decide
how to optimise the joint strategy of the coalition. Solving
the optimisation problem centrally raises similar information
sharing concerns to Algorithm 1, as it requires full informa-
tion from all agents. To address this, we adopt a distributed
solution based on ADMM [11], which enables agents to com-
pute their local decisions while coordinating only through
limited information exchange. We reformulate the coalition
optimisation problem in a consensus form, allowing each
agent to solve a local subproblem while enforcing agreement
on shared variables through a coordinator.

i, representing the consensus coalition trade schedule across

V. NUMERICALRESULTS
We make use of a real-world dataset [15], [16] to perform
experiments, with energy usage recorded for 15-minute time
slots, predictions for both generation and demand, battery
data and energy prices taken from this dataset1. Whenever
we seek to solve (9) forV(C |), we perform ADMM until the
primal residual is less than 10−5, and use a penalty parameter
c=1
2. The experiments, therefore, focus on assessing the
impact of limited-information coalition formation, rather than
differences in the underlying optimisation solver. We use a
coalition size limit that allows computations to be completed
within a reasonable time frame, while offering reasonable
cost reductions (for our limited information approach, we
compare different coalition sizes in Section V-D). All simu-
lations were performed using 2 CPU cores at 2.6 GHz and
4 GB RAM.
A. Open Loop Optimisation
Results are presented in Table I for the open loop optimisa-
tion problem using first all 70 buildings, and then 8 buildings,
with a maximum coalition size of 7 buildings, and planning
for a single day ahead. For 70 agents, the optimal coalition
problem was terminated after being unable to find a solution
within 24 hours.
As can be seen, our algorithm offers an improvement over

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This document proposes a new algorithm for coalition formation in local energy management systems, specifically for distributed energy systems with prosumers. The main points covered are:

*   **Problem:** Existing bottom-up coalition formation methods for energy management require full information sharing, leading to privacy concerns and high computational overhead.
*   **Proposed Solution:** A limited information coalition-formation algorithm that only requires the exchange of aggregate information. This is achieved by constructing an upper bound on the value of candidate coalitions, avoiding the need to solve full optimization problems for each potential merge.
*   **Benefits:**
    *   Significantly reduces computational complexity.
    *   Limits information exchange, preserving agent privacy.
    *   Guarantees that the resulting cost is no greater than that of decentralized operation.
*   **Methodology:**
    *   Coalition strategies are optimized using a distributed approach based on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM).
    *   The framework is embedded within a Model Predictive Control (MPC) scheme.
*   **Evaluation:** The approach is evaluated on real-world data, demonstrating improved economic performance over decentralized control and lower computational cost compared to full-information methods.
*   **Contributions:**
    *   A coalition formation algorithm that avoids solving optimization problems for candidate merges by using an efficiently computable upper bound on coalition value.
    *   A method requiring only aggregate grid trade information, enhancing privacy.
    *   A proof of cost optimality relative to decentralized operation.
    *   Integration with ADMM and MPC.
    *   Numerical results showing improved performance and reduced computational cost.
*   **Generalizability:** The technique is presented as generally applicable to all trading games, with potential extensions to trade-off optimality and information sharing.

structure.title: Building Model
structure.summary: The document discusses a method for forming coalitions of buildings to optimize energy trading and reduce costs. It contrasts a "full information" approach, which requires sharing all optimization variables and constraints, with a "limited information" approach that only shares planned grid trades. The proposed limited-information method aims to reduce information sharing and preserve agent privacy by requiring only aggregate grid trade information. The document outlines the building model, including demand, generation, battery dynamics, and energy trading with the grid. It also introduces the concept of coalitions as disjoint partitions of buildings that can trade energy freely among themselves. The core problem addressed is forming an optimal coalition structure to minimize the total cost of operation, with the guarantee that the resulting structure's cost will not exceed that of decentralized operation. The method is integrated with distributed optimization techniques like ADMM and model predictive control, and numerical results on real-world data are presented to demonstrate its improved performance and lower computational cost compared to existing methods. The technique is presented as generally applicable to all trading games, with potential extensions to balance optimality and information sharing.

structure.summary:

*   **Coalition Formation:** The core problem is to determine the optimal structure of coalitions to minimize overall energy costs.
*   **Information Sharing:** A key aspect is the trade-off between the level of information shared and the optimality of the coalition structure. Full-information methods require sharing all optimization variables and constraints, while a proposed limited-information approach only shares planned grid trades.
*   **Limited Information Approach:** This approach reduces information sharing, preserving agent privacy and computational burden. It relies on an efficiently computable upper bound on coalition value.
*   **Algorithm:** A bottom-up coalition formation algorithm is presented, which iteratively merges coalitions if it leads to a cost reduction.
*   **Guarantees:** The proposed limited-information method guarantees that the resulting coalition structure's total cost will not exceed that of decentralized operation.
*   **Integration:** The coalition formation scheme is integrated with distributed optimization techniques like ADMM and a model predictive control framework.
*   **Numerical Results:** Real-world data demonstrates improved performance over decentralized control and lower computational cost compared to full-information methods.
*   **General Applicability:** The technique is applicable to all trading games, with potential extensions to balance optimality and information sharing.
*   **Building Model:** A detailed model of individual buildings is provided, including demand, generation, battery dynamics, and trading with the grid.
*   **Optimization Problems:** The document defines open-loop optimization problems for individual buildings and for coalitions.
*   **Practical Bound Calculation:** A specific method for calculating a non-trivial upper bound on coalition cost using only aggregate grid trade information is detailed. This bound is based on identifying time steps where one coalition is buying from the grid and another is selling.

structure.title: Coalitions
structure.summary: This partial document discusses a trade-off between information sharing and optimality in coalition formation. It introduces an assumption that the exact value of a formed coalition can be evaluated. A theorem is presented regarding the properties of a "Limited Information Algorithm," which uses an upper bound on joint costs instead of solving an optimization problem. The algorithm is proven to result in a valid coalition structure, terminate finitely, and achieve a value at most equal to the decentralized optimum. The document then proposes a practical and computationally cheap method for obtaining this upper bound by sharing planned net grid trades. This method involves calculating the total grid trade for coalitions and identifying time steps where one coalition buys and another sells. A formula is derived for the upper bound on coalition cost based on potential trades between coalitions. Finally, a corollary and its proof demonstrate that this bound is non-trivial and achievable by explicitly constructing a feasible coalition strategy.

structure.title: COALITIONFORMATION
structure.summary:
The document discusses optimizing energy trading within a coalition of buildings. It introduces new optimization variables for buying and selling energy within a coalition, amending power balance equations and constraint sets. The core problem involves minimizing the cumulative cost of all agents by optimizing coalition structures.

The document explores two main approaches for coalition formation:

1.  **Optimal (Size-Limited) Coalition:** This involves directly finding the true optimal coalition structure, which is formulated as a mixed-integer linear program. However, this approach is computationally expensive due to the combinatorial nature of exploring all possible partitions.

2.  **Bottom-Up Coalition Formation:** This is a less computationally intensive, approximate approach that iteratively merges existing coalitions. It avoids exhaustive enumeration by evaluating pairwise merges. However, this method requires sharing full local information for each potential coalition merge.

To address the information sharing drawback of the bottom-up approach, a **Limited Information Coalition Formation** strategy is proposed. This method uses an upper bound on the coalition's cost instead of the exact value, allowing for reduced information sharing. The document details how to calculate a practical and non-trivial upper bound by comparing planned net grid trades of potential merging coalitions. This trade-off allows agents to balance information sharing with optimality. The algorithm's properties, including termination and the resulting coalition structure's value, are analyzed.

nodes.title: Limited Information Coalition Formation
nodes.summary:
This document excerpt discusses algorithms and assumptions related to coalition formation and optimization in a decentralized system, likely for energy management. Key points include:

*   **Trade-off between Information Sharing and Optimality:** Agents face a choice between sharing more information to achieve better coalition structures and maintaining privacy.
*   **Assumption on Coalition Value Knowledge:** Once a coalition is formed, its exact value can be determined.
*   **Properties of a Limited Information Algorithm:** A specific algorithm (Algorithm 1) is analyzed, showing it produces valid coalition structures, terminates finitely, and achieves a value at most equal to the decentralized optimum, even with upper bounds on coalition costs.
*   **Practical Bound for Coalition Cost:** A computationally efficient method is proposed to calculate a non-trivial upper bound for coalition costs by sharing only planned net grid trades. This bound is shown to be achievable.
*   **Within Coalition Optimization:** A distributed optimization approach using ADMM is presented to optimize the joint strategy of a coalition without requiring full information sharing from all agents. This method allows agents to solve local subproblems while coordinating through limited information exchange.
*   **Model Predictive Control (MPC) Framework:** The developed methods are integrated into an MPC framework. This involves using predicted consumption and generation profiles to solve open-loop optimization problems at each time step.
*   **Dynamic Coalition Formation in MPC:** Coalitions are reformed at every time step to adapt to changing conditions. A condition is enforced to ensure that any formed coalition does not perform worse than individual agents working separately.
*   **Theorem on MPC with Coalition Formation:** It is proven that even with dynamic coalition reformation, the total cost in the coalitional MPC framework is less than or equal to the decentralized MPC approach.

nodes.title: Within Coalition Optimisation
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses two main topics: within-coalition optimization and the application of these methods within a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework.

For **within-coalition optimization**, the document proposes a distributed solution using ADMM (Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers) to address information sharing concerns. This approach allows agents within a coalition to optimize their joint strategy by solving local subproblems and coordinating through limited information exchange, specifically focusing on consensus variables representing trade schedules. The method ensures feasibility by adjusting local grid trades after ADMM convergence to restore power balance.

In the context of **Model Predictive Control (MPC)**, the document explains how the previously discussed open-loop optimization methods are integrated into an MPC framework. This involves using predicted consumption and generation profiles to solve the optimization problem at each time step. The document highlights that coalitions are reformed dynamically at every time step. A key aspect is the condition for coalition dissolution: if a coalition's cost exceeds the sum of individual agent costs, it is dissolved, and agents revert to individual operation. This mechanism guarantees that the MPC approach with coalition formation performs no worse than the decentralized optimum. A theorem is presented to formally state this performance guarantee.
